435.title: Bamidbar: wrap the holy things (Numbers 4:5–20)
435.hook: the holiest objects are carefully covered before travel
435.howItsDone: Synagogues keep the Torah scroll dressed in a cloth mantle, often with a breastplate and crowns, and cover it between readings; worn-out scrolls and prayer books are not thrown away but stored in a genizah and buried.

segments.voice: Yesterday Moses was counted a parent because he taught. Your line was teachers are parents too. Today, moving day in the wilderness.

Watch someone pack a grandmother's china for a move. Every plate gets its own sheet of paper. Cups go in separately, handles turned in. The box is labeled in big letters, this side up, and nobody is allowed to throw it in the back of the truck with the folding chairs. Moving day shows you what a family treasures. In the wilderness, the whole sanctuary has to move every time the cloud lifts. Numbers chapter four is the packing list, and its care shows how holy things were held.
screen: `EVERY PLATE ITS OWN PAPER.` → `THIS SIDE UP.` → `THE SANCTUARY'S PACKING LIST.`

segments.voice: When the camp is ready to set out, Aaron and his sons go into the sanctuary first. They take down the curtain that screened off the holiest place and wrap the ark of the covenant in it. Over that, a covering of skins. Over that, a cloth all of blue. The table of showbread, with its dishes and bread, gets its own cloths. The lampstand, its lamps and tongs, wrapped and set on a carrying frame. The golden altar, the utensils, the bronze altar: each in turn. Only then are the carriers called in: the Levite clan of Kohath, who carry the holiest objects on their shoulders, by poles. But the text sets two limits. They must not touch the holy things themselves. And they must not go in to watch the holy things being covered, even for a moment; the verse says plainly it would cost them their lives. Aaron's sons are told to appoint each carrier to his task and his load, one by one, so nobody wanders where he shouldn't. Some commentators read this as protection, not distrust. The priests wrap; the Levites carry; each is guarded by the order. The holiest things travel unseen, swaddled in blue, carried with care through dust and heat. Jewish practice still treats holy things with that kind of tenderness. A Torah scroll is dressed in a cover between readings. A worn-out scroll or prayer book isn't thrown away; it's buried.

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your life that deserves more care than it gets: a letter, a photo, a ring kept loose in a drawer, or something that isn't an object at all, a friend's secret, your hours of sleep, a child's trust. Picture wrapping it, layer by layer, the way the priests wrapped the ark. What would the first layer be, and the second?
Bamidbar, the wilderness book, and the last day of its first portion: the holy things wrapped in blue before the journey.
Your line: cover what's holy. Care can be its own kind of reverence. That's day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: Naso: lift up the heads (Numbers 4:22)
436.hook: the census phrase means both "count" and "lift up"
436.howItsDone: Naso is read in late spring, usually just after Shavuot. Its opening phrase, naso et rosh, is studied as a lesson in how being counted can lift a person up.

segments.voice: Yesterday the holy things were wrapped in blue for the road. Your line was cover what's holy. Today, a new portion.

In prison, in Genesis, Joseph listens to two men's dreams. To the royal cupbearer he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, and give you back your job. To the royal baker he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, too. Then he finishes the sentence. Off you. The same Hebrew phrase, lift up the head, means a pardon for one man and a hanging for the other. Hold on to that phrase. It comes back in this week's portion, and this time it's about counting.
screen: `TWO DREAMS IN PRISON.` → `LIFT UP YOUR HEAD.` → `A PARDON, OR A HANGING.`

segments.voice: The new portion is called Naso, from its first instruction. God tells Moses to take the sum of the sons of Gershon. In Hebrew: naso et rosh, literally, lift up the head. It's a phrase the Torah uses for taking a census. You don't count heads; you lift them. The phrase has the double edge Joseph's dreams show. Being counted can raise you up, or it can single you out. Some read the census itself as a choice about which it will be. To count someone well is to lift them: you matter, you're on the list, you belong. Then look at who's being counted. Gershon is named first among Levi's sons. Yet in the order of service, Kohath, the younger clan, was counted first, because Kohath carried the ark. Gershon's clan carried the curtains, the coverings, the hangings and the ropes. Soft goods. Not glamorous. And the verse adds two small Hebrew words: gam hem, them also. Take the sum of the sons of Gershon too. Some commentators read those words as a deliberate lift for the clan that might have felt second. They count. Their load counts. The same root, nun, sin, alef, lift or carry, turns up again in these chapters as the word for bearing the sanctuary's loads. It'll come back soon, in a blessing, when God lifts up a face. In Naso, to count is to carry, and to carry is to lift.

Naso. Lift up: the word this week's portion is named for, the Bible's way of saying count, and its way of saying you matter.
Your line: counting is lifting. Them also: no one's load goes uncounted. Day four hundred thirty-six.

437.title: Naso: confess and repay (Numbers 5:6–7)
437.hook: a wrong is confessed aloud and repaid with a fifth added
437.howItsDone: Jewish tradition sees verbal confession, vidui, as part of repentance; on Yom Kippur the congregation recites the confessions together, aloud and in the plural, and wrongs against people are repaired by making restitution and seeking their forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naso, lift up the head. Your line was counting is lifting. Today, how a wrong gets fixed.

You borrowed your neighbor's ladder in March and it's now October. Or you dinged a friend's car door in a parking lot and drove off, and it's been nagging at you for a year. You could quietly return the ladder. You could slip some cash in an envelope. It's tempting to fix things in a way that skips saying anything out loud. Today's verses in Naso include two steps that are easy to skip. One of them is your mouth. The other is your wallet, plus a little.
screen: `A LADDER KEPT SINCE MARCH.` → `FIX IT QUIETLY?` → `YOUR MOUTH, AND A LITTLE EXTRA.`

segments.voice: Numbers five, verses six and seven. When a man or a woman wrongs another person, the Torah calls it a trespass against the LORD. Notice that: cheating your neighbor isn't only between the two of you. Then the remedy: "then they shall confess their sin which they have done." After that, they repay the full amount, add a fifth on top, and give it to the person they wronged. Two steps, in order. First, the mouth. Then the money. The verse's verb is vehitvadu, they shall confess, and from it comes the name for this first step: vidui, confession, owning it. Maimonides builds a whole teaching on this verse. Real repentance, he writes, includes saying it in words: I did this, I regret it, I'm ashamed of it, I won't do it again. Thinking it isn't enough. The words make it real, to you as much as anyone. On Yom Kippur, the confessions are said aloud, together, in the plural: we have sinned, we have done wrong. Then the fifth. Returning what you took only puts things back where they were. The added fifth admits the other person lost more than an object: time, trust, sleep, the use of their ladder all summer. The rabbis worked out the arithmetic: the fifth is counted so that it's a fifth of the total you hand over. And if the wronged person has died with no relatives, the verse says, the payment doesn't vanish. It goes to the priest. A debt like this doesn't just expire.

segments.voice: Look for one small wrong you still owe for, the ladder, a forgotten favor, a cutting remark, and picture the person. Then think of the fifth, the extra that admits their loss: a coffee with the returned book, a full tank with the borrowed car.
Vidui. Confession: owning a wrong out loud, the first step before repaying it, and the root of the Yom Kippur prayers.
Your line: repay, and add a fifth. Owning it out loud comes first. Four hundred thirty-seven days now.

438.title: Naso: the nazirite (Numbers 6:1–21)
438.hook: a person may vow to give up wine and haircuts for a season
438.howItsDone: The nazirite vow, described in Numbers 6 and the Mishnah's tractate Nazir, depended on the Temple's offerings and is not practiced today; Jewish teachers still discuss it as a model, and a warning, about holy self-denial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vidui, confession out loud. Your line was repay, and add a fifth. Today, a vow with an end date.

Dry January. A month without social media. No sugar until the wedding. A beard grown out for a cause. A fixed-term vow is a familiar idea: something hard, something visible, with an end date circled on the calendar. The Torah has one too, with rules, a start, an end, and a ceremony to close it. You'd spot this person in a crowd. Long hair, never cut for the whole season. A cup of water where everyone else is drinking wine. Numbers chapter six calls them the nazirite.
screen: `DRY JANUARY. NO SUGAR TILL THE WEDDING.` → `A VOW WITH AN END DATE.` → `THE NAZIRITE.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens: when either a man or a woman makes a special vow to be a nazir, set apart for the LORD. Man or woman: anyone could take this vow. Then three rules. No wine and nothing from grapes, not even raisins, seeds or skins. No razor on the head; the hair grows wild for the whole term. And no contact with the dead, not even at the funeral of one's own parents. The verse says the nazirite is holy to the LORD for all those days. Nazir means one set apart. The verse calls what's on the nazirite's head the nezer, the consecration, a word that elsewhere means a crown. If no length is named, the Mishnah says the vow runs thirty days. At the end the nazirite brings offerings, shaves the head at the sanctuary door, and puts the hair on the fire. Then, the verse says, they may drink wine again. The vow was always for a season. Here's where it gets interesting. One of those closing offerings is a sin offering. Why would someone who gave things up for God need atonement? The Talmud keeps two answers side by side. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: because they denied themselves wine, which God made good. If refusing wine needs atonement, how much more refusing everything. Other sages point to the verse itself: the nazirite shall be holy. Both views stay on the page. A vow can lift you, and it can also curdle into scorn for ordinary life. The Torah gives it an end date.

Nazir. Set apart: the person who vows, for a season, no wine, no haircut and no contact with the dead.

439.title: Naso: the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
439.hook: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee", still said over children and congregations
439.tomorrow: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)
439.howItsDone: Kohanim, descendants of Aaron, chant the priestly blessing with raised hands in synagogue: daily in the Land of Israel and in many Sephardic communities, on festivals in many Ashkenazi communities elsewhere. Many parents say it over their children on Friday night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nazir, set apart by a vow with an end date. Your line was a vow for a season. Today, three lines from this book that are still said aloud every week.

Friday night, in a lot of Jewish homes, before the meal. A parent puts both hands on a child's head. The child might be four and wriggling, seventeen and rolling their eyes, or thirty and home for the weekend. The parent says a few quiet words, the same every week. In a synagogue in Jerusalem, every morning, a row of men with prayer shawls over their heads lift their hands toward the congregation and chant those very words. They come from today's portion, and they're three lines long.
screen: `HANDS ON A CHILD'S HEAD.` → `A ROW OF RAISED HANDS.` → `THE SAME THREE LINES.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses to give Aaron and his sons these words for blessing the people. "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." In Hebrew it's Birkat Kohanim, the blessing of the priests. Count the Hebrew words and they grow: three, then five, then seven, like a breath getting deeper. The first line asks for blessing and protection, the things that keep a life safe. The second asks for God's face to shine: warmth, favor, grace. The third asks God to lift up a face toward you, the same root as naso, lift, and ends with shalom, peace. Right after, the Torah adds that the priests shall put God's name upon the people, and God will bless them. The priests speak, but it is God who blesses. The kohanim are a channel, not the source. Descendants of Aaron, kohanim, still say it today: every day in Israel, and on festivals in many synagogues outside Israel. They raise their hands with fingers spread, prayer shawls over their heads, and the congregation lowers its eyes. At home on Friday night, parents say it over their children. The words are old outside the Bible, too. In 1979, archaeologists near Jerusalem found two tiny silver scrolls, rolled up like amulets, centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. Inscribed on them: a version of this blessing.

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, a child, a friend, a parent, someone far away or struggling, and picture their face. If they don't, simply hold the person in mind and wish them safety, warmth and peace.
Birkat Kohanim. The priestly blessing: three lines that grow from three words to seven, ending in peace.

440.title: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)
440.hook: each tribal leader brings an identical gift, and each is listed in full
440.howItsDone: Numbers 7, the gifts of the tribal leaders, is read in synagogue as part of Naso and again, a day at a time, during the eight days of Hanukkah, the festival of dedication.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Kohanim: three lines that grow from three words to seven, and end in peace. Your line was bless thee, and keep thee. Today, the end of Naso.

At a graduation, the dean reads every single name. Three hundred students, and each one walks across the stage, shakes the same hand, takes the same rolled-up paper. It takes forever. Somebody in the back row checks their phone. Wouldn't it be faster to say congratulations, everyone? Sure. But ask any parent in the audience whether it's the same. Numbers chapter seven makes the slow choice on purpose, twelve times in a row, and the chapter grows long because of it.
screen: `EVERY NAME READ ALOUD.` → `THE SAME HANDSHAKE, 300 TIMES.` → `THE SLOW CHOICE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The Tabernacle is finished and anointed, and the leaders of the twelve tribes come forward to dedicate the altar. Each leader is called a nasi, from the same root as naso: one who is lifted up. They bring their gifts one per day, for twelve days. On the first day, Nachshon, of Judah: one silver dish and one silver basin, both full of fine flour mixed with oil; one golden pan full of incense; a bull, a ram, a lamb, a goat, and more for the peace offerings. On the second day, the leader of Issachar brings exactly the same. And the third. Down to the shekel. And the Torah writes it out every time: twelve paragraphs, almost word for word, then a grand total. Eighty-nine verses. An editor might cut it. The commentators asked why it stays. Nachmanides answers that God wanted to honor each leader equally. Each chose to bring the gift on his own day, and the Torah wouldn't let anyone be summarized as the same as the one before. A midrash goes further: the gifts were identical, but each leader had his own meaning in mind, tied to his own tribe's story. Same silver, different hearts. This chapter is also read in synagogue during Hanukkah, because its theme is dedication. The Hebrew for dedication of the altar is chanukat hamizbe'ach. Hanukkah is the same word.

441.title: Beha'alotcha: until it rises alone (Numbers 8:2)
441.hook: Rashi: Aaron holds the light to the wick until the flame rises by itself
441.howItsDone: Beha'alotcha is read in early summer; Rashi's comments on its first verse, that the flame must be held until it rises by itself, and that Aaron's tending of the lamps outshone the leaders' gifts, are often taught as a picture of teaching and patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve leaders brought twelve identical gifts, each one written out in full. Your line was each gift counted in full.

A birthday cake, a draft from the window, one match. You touch the match to the wick. The wick blackens, smokes, takes a tiny blue bead of flame. Pull the match away too soon and it dies. So you wait, holding steady, until the flame stands up on its own and doesn't need you anymore. Then you let go. That small, patient moment is how the commentator Rashi explains the word this week's portion is named for, and it becomes a picture of what a teacher does.
screen: `A MATCH TO A WICK.` → `TOO SOON, IT DIES.` → `WAIT TILL IT STANDS ALONE.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses to speak to Aaron: "When thou lightest the lamps," the seven lamps of the menorah shall give light toward its front. In Hebrew, when thou lightest is beha'alotcha, and it doesn't literally say light. It says when you raise up, when you make it go up. Rashi asks why. His answer, from the ancient rabbis: because the flame goes upward. Aaron must hold the light to each wick until the flame rises by itself. Rashi's second comment connects to yesterday. Why does this section come right after the leaders' twelve gifts? Because, the midrash says, Aaron felt left out. Every tribe had a leader at the dedication, and his tribe, Levi, brought nothing. So God told him: yours is greater than theirs. They brought gifts once. You will light and tend the lamps. A gift is given and done; a flame has to be kept. Then the verse says simply: and Aaron did so. Rashi reads that as praise: he didn't change a thing, day after day. The image is often borrowed for teaching. You don't light someone by grabbing their wick and holding it forever, or by touching it once and walking away. You stay close, steady, until the light is theirs. Then you step back, and the flame keeps going up.
screen: `BEHA'ALOTCHA: WHEN YOU RAISE UP.` · `HOLD IT TILL IT RISES ALONE.` · `A GIFT IS ONCE. A FLAME IS KEPT.` · `AND AARON DID SO.` · then, large: `UNTIL IT RISES ALONE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone just starting something: a kid learning to cook, a new coworker, a friend trying to quit something, a student stuck on a problem. Ask honestly whether you pull the match away too soon, or hold it there so long it never becomes theirs. Picture one way to stay close a little longer, and one way to let go a little sooner.

Beha'alotcha. When you raise up: the lamp held until it burns alone. This week: cover what's holy, counting is lifting, repay and add a fifth, a vow for a season, the priests' blessing, each gift counted in full, and now this.
Your line: until it rises alone. The light was always meant to be theirs. That's four hundred forty-one days.
